problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cosh}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{cosh}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?

activity_context.topic_title: Surface Areas of Revolution for Parametric Curves

examples.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of Y
examples.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = \sin t, \quad y = e^t, \quad t\in \left[0,1\right].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?
examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2}+1,\,y={t}^{3},\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
feedback.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})=3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\sqrt{{t}^{2}(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{(4+9{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot |t|\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\cdot t\cdot \sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{4}\sqrt{9{t}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
